unit.title: The Kitchen
unit.summary: The non-volley zone: volleys, the line, momentum, when you may enter.

lessons.title: What the kitchen is
lessons.objective: Define the non-volley zone and its line.

payload.prompt: Match kitchen terms to their meanings.

pairs.definition: The friendly nickname for the 7-foot strip beside the net on each side
The official rulebook name, because you cannot volley there
The line at the far edge of the zone; it counts as part of the zone

distractorDefinitions: The service box where you stand to serve
The area you must reach to win a point

explanation.summary: The kitchen is the 7-foot strip on each side of the net where volleys are forbidden, officially the non-volley zone (NVZ). The kitchen line marks its far edge and counts as kitchen.
explanation.sayThisLine: The kitchen is the 7-foot no-volley zone on each side.

payload.prompt: How far from the net is the kitchen on each side?

options.text: 3 feet
7 feet
10 feet
15 feet

explanation.correct: The kitchen reaches 7 feet from the net on each side, so the two kitchens together span 14 feet across the middle of the court.
explanation.incorrect: It is 7 feet, the same on both sides of the net. That is far enough back that you cannot stand at the net and smash, but close enough that dinks still matter.
explanation.sayThisLine: The kitchen is 7 feet from the net on each side.

payload.prompt: Complete the kitchen definition.
payload.template: The kitchen is a {{area}} zone {{distance}} from the net on {{sides}}.

explanation.correct: The kitchen is a no-volley zone, 7 feet from the net, on each side. You can stand in it and hit bounced balls; you just can't volley.
explanation.incorrect: The kitchen is on both sides of the net (not just one), exactly 7 feet deep, and named for the no-volley rule that applies there.
explanation.sayThisLine: 7-foot no-volley zone, each side of the net.

payload.prompt: A ball bounces 9 feet from the net. Is it in the kitchen?

scene.alt: Top-down court view showing a ball landing 9 feet from the net, just past the kitchen line.

explanation.correct: Not in the kitchen. The kitchen reaches 7 feet from the net, so a ball 9 feet out is in open court, past the kitchen line.
explanation.incorrect: The kitchen is only 7 feet deep. A ball bouncing at 9 feet is two feet beyond the kitchen line, in regular court.
explanation.sayThisLine: Past the kitchen line, it is regular court.

lessons.title: What is a volley?
lessons.objective: Distinguish a volley from a groundstroke.

payload.prompt: What makes a shot a volley?

options.text: You hit it hard and fast
You hit it before it bounces
You stand near the net
You use a certain grip

explanation.correct: A volley is any shot hit in the air before the ball bounces. The ball doesn't touch the court before you strike it.
explanation.incorrect: Volleying is defined by the timing: the ball is still in flight when you hit it. Speed, position, and grip don't define it.
explanation.sayThisLine: A volley is hitting the ball in the air before it bounces.

payload.prompt: The ball bounced once on your side. You hit it on the way up.

scene.alt: You stand near the baseline and hit a ball that has already bounced once on your side.

explanation.correct: Not a volley. A volley is a ball hit before it bounces, and this one already bounced. Hitting it after a bounce is a groundstroke.
explanation.incorrect: The bounce is what matters. If the ball has touched the court, hitting it afterwards is not a volley, whatever the height or speed.
explanation.sayThisLine: If it already bounced, it is not a volley.

payload.prompt: A slow ball floats in the air. Your feet are outside the kitchen.

situation.narrative: You are standing a step behind the kitchen line. A slow ball drifts toward you in the air, about waist high.

facts.label: Your feet
facts.value: Outside the kitchen, clear of the line

facts.label: The ball
facts.value: Still in the air, has not bounced

options.label: Volley it from where you stand
options.consequence: Legal and sensible. You are outside the kitchen, so a volley is allowed, and taking it out of the air gives the other side less time.
considerations: Your feet are clear of the kitchen
A volley is just a ball hit before it bounces
Less time for the other side to reset

options.label: Step into the kitchen, then volley it
options.consequence: Kitchen fault. Volleying while standing in the kitchen is exactly what the zone forbids.
considerations: Your feet would be inside the zone
You would lose the point
You could wait for the bounce instead

options.label: Let it bounce, then hit it
options.consequence: Also legal. It gives you a bit more time, but a short bounce might drag you toward the kitchen and the other side gets time to reset.
considerations: Always legal, in or out of the kitchen
More time to set your feet
Gives the other side time to recover

payload.expertNote: Volleying is fine anywhere outside the kitchen. Whether to volley or wait is a judgment call, and it comes with practice.
payload.sayThisLine: I can volley from out here, just not from in the kitchen.

payload.prompt: Complete the volley definition.
payload.template: A volley is a shot where the ball is hit {{when}} it {{touches}}.

explanation.correct: A volley is hit before the ball touches the court. Once it bounces, any shot is a groundstroke or a return.
explanation.incorrect: The key to a volley is that the ball never bounces. You strike it in the air, before impact with the court.
explanation.sayThisLine: Volley = hit before bounce. Groundstroke = hit after bounce.

lessons.title: No volleys in the kitchen
lessons.objective: Call fair vs faulty volleys with feet on court.

payload.prompt: You are standing with both feet in the kitchen and you volley the ball.

scene.alt: You stand with feet inside the kitchen zone, volleying a ball.

explanation.correct: Kitchen fault. You cannot volley while standing in the kitchen, no matter how good the shot looks.
explanation.incorrect: The rule is simple: no volleys in the kitchen, period. Your feet position determines it, and both are in the zone.
explanation.sayThisLine: Feet in the kitchen = no volley. That's a fault.

payload.prompt: You stand just outside the kitchen and volley. Is that legal?

options.text: No, you are still near the kitchen
Yes, if you are not touching the kitchen or its line
Only if the ball is above the net
Only on your first volley

explanation.correct: Legal. The rule is about touching the kitchen, line included. Outside it you can volley as often as you like.
explanation.incorrect: Being near the kitchen does not matter, and neither does ball height or how many volleys you have hit. What counts is whether you are touching the zone or its line.
explanation.sayThisLine: Near the kitchen is fine. In it or on its line is not.

payload.prompt: Match the foot position to the call.

pairs.definition: Kitchen fault; you cannot volley from there

pairs.term: One foot in, one foot out
pairs.definition: Kitchen fault; one foot in (or on the line) is enough
Legal to volley; foot position is clear

distractorDefinitions: Legal only if the ball is below the net
Legal only if it is a soft shot

explanation.summary: A kitchen fault happens when you volley while touching the kitchen or its line. One foot is enough. Volleying with both feet clear of the zone is the legal position.
explanation.sayThisLine: Any foot in the kitchen = fault. Both out = legal.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I was standing in the kitchen and I hit a perfect volley. They called it a fault.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: That's the rule: no volleys in the kitchen, even perfect ones.
If it was perfect, it should count.
They must have misjudged where you were standing.
The kitchen rule is too strict.

payload.translation: Sam was standing in the kitchen when the ball was volleyed, which is the one thing the rule forbids. How good the shot was does not change the call.

followUps.line: Ouch, that stings. The rule only cares where your feet were, not how good the shot was.
followUps.why: Sympathizes first, then names the rule.

followUps.line: It is a harsh one. You can go into the kitchen, you just have to let the ball bounce first.
followUps.why: Shows Sam the way out instead of arguing the call.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Sam is probably a little annoyed. Start with sympathy, then the rule, and skip the lecture.

lessons.title: The line counts as kitchen
lessons.objective: Recognize a toe on the line as in the kitchen.

payload.prompt: Tap the area where a volley fault occurs if your foot lands there.

diagram.alt: Top-down pickleball court showing the kitchen zones and the kitchen line.

explanation.correct: Both the line and the space inside are kitchen. A foot on either one means you cannot volley from there.
explanation.incorrect: The kitchen line is part of the kitchen for volley rules. Touching the line is the same as being inside, and only the open court behind it is fair for volleys.
explanation.sayThisLine: Kitchen line counts as kitchen when volleying.

payload.prompt: Your toe touches the kitchen line and you volley.

scene.alt: You stand with one toe touching the kitchen line, volleying the ball.

explanation.correct: Kitchen fault. The line itself counts as kitchen. A toe on the line is the same as a foot in the zone.
explanation.incorrect: Many people think the line is safe, but it isn't. For volley rules, the line = kitchen.
explanation.sayThisLine: Toe on the kitchen line = kitchen fault.

payload.ruleTag: Kitchen line is part of the kitchen

payload.prompt: If your foot is exactly on the kitchen line and you volley, is it legal?

options.text: Yes, the line itself is neutral territory
No, the line counts as kitchen for volleys
Only if you're moving backward
Only if the ball is above your head

explanation.correct: The line counts as kitchen. A foot touching the line is a kitchen fault when volleying.
explanation.incorrect: Unlike some sports, in pickleball the kitchen line is not a neutral boundary. It's part of the kitchen.
explanation.sayThisLine: Kitchen line counts as kitchen; touching it = fault when volleying.

payload.prompt: You want to volley. Where should your front foot land?

situation.narrative: You are two feet behind the kitchen line, and a ball is coming in the air that you want to volley.

facts.label: Where you are
facts.value: Two feet behind the kitchen line

facts.label: The ball
facts.value: In the air, reachable with one more step

facts.label: The worry
facts.value: Your front foot landing on the line

options.label: Step up so your toe lands right on the kitchen line
options.consequence: Kitchen fault. The line counts as kitchen, so volleying with a toe on it is illegal.
considerations: The line itself counts as kitchen
You would lose the rally with a fault
There is no benefit in stepping that close

options.label: Stop with both feet clearly behind the line, then volley
options.consequence: Legal. Both feet are clear of the line, so the volley is fine and there is no doubt about the call.
considerations: Clear foot position leaves no doubt
You can still reach most balls from here
A little space gives margin for your momentum

payload.expertNote: Leave a little room behind the line when you volley. A toe on the line is the most common way people fault without meaning to.
payload.sayThisLine: A toe on the line is still in the kitchen.

lessons.title: The momentum trap
lessons.objective: Judge a volley followed by momentum into the zone.

payload.prompt: You volley from outside the kitchen, but your forward momentum carries your foot into the zone after you hit the ball.

scene.alt: You are shown volleying from outside the kitchen, with an arrow indicating your forward momentum.

explanation.correct: Momentum fault. Starting outside the kitchen is not enough: if your momentum carries you into the zone after the volley, it is still a fault, even if the ball is already past your opponent.
explanation.incorrect: The volley is judged from contact until you have stopped. Your momentum carrying you or your footing into the kitchen counts against you.
explanation.sayThisLine: Momentum into the kitchen after volleying = fault.

payload.prompt: Why does the momentum rule exist?

options.text: To punish players who move slowly
So a player cannot volley from the edge and glide into the kitchen
To stop players from running forward at all
To protect the court surface

explanation.correct: Without it, a player could sprint in, volley at the last moment and let their body carry them into the zone, getting the benefit of a volley from right at the net. The rule closes that loophole.
explanation.incorrect: The rule is not about speed or the floor. It keeps the kitchen rule honest by counting the whole volley, including where your momentum takes you.
explanation.sayThisLine: The momentum rule closes the loophole of volleying and gliding in.

payload.prompt: You are a foot behind the kitchen line, about to volley. What now?

situation.narrative: A ball is coming in the air and you are running forward to reach it, one foot behind the kitchen line.

facts.label: Your position
facts.value: One foot behind the kitchen line

facts.label: The risk
facts.value: Momentum carrying you into the kitchen

options.label: Lunge into the volley and let your body follow through
options.consequence: Likely momentum fault. If your foot or body ends up in the kitchen after the volley, it is called, even if the shot was great.
considerations: The fault counts what happens after contact
You are only a foot from the line
A great shot does not cancel the fault

options.label: Brake early, hit the volley, and stay balanced behind the line
options.consequence: Legal. Stopping your feet before you hit keeps your whole body out of the kitchen, so the volley stands.
considerations: Balance matters more than reach here
You stay outside the zone after contact
You can step forward once the point is over

payload.expertNote: Good volleyers slow their feet before they hit. You do not need a big swing to make a good volley, just a steady base.
payload.sayThisLine: I stop my feet before I volley so I do not drift in.

lessons.title: When you can go in
lessons.objective: Know you may enter to hit a bounced ball; must exit before volleying.

payload.prompt: A ball bounces in the kitchen. Can you go in to hit it?

situation.narrative: Your opponent hits a short shot that lands in your kitchen and has already bounced once.

facts.label: Ball location
facts.value: Bounced once, sitting in the kitchen

facts.label: Your action
facts.value: Stepping into the zone to reach it

facts.label: Next action
facts.value: Hitting the ball after its bounce

options.label: Step into the kitchen and hit it after the bounce
options.consequence: Legal. You can go into the kitchen any time to hit a ball that has bounced. The rule only bans volleys from inside it.
considerations: A ball that has bounced can be hit from anywhere
You can stand in the kitchen, just not volley there
Short balls are often only reachable this way

options.label: Stay back and wait for a second bounce
options.consequence: You lose the point. A ball may bounce only once on your side before you must hit it, and you can go in to hit it.
considerations: A second bounce ends the rally
You were allowed to step in
Waiting is never a safe option here

payload.expertNote: The kitchen is not off limits. You can walk in whenever you like. You just cannot volley from there, so stepping in for a bounced ball is perfectly fine.
payload.sayThisLine: I can step into the kitchen for a ball that has bounced.

payload.prompt: Still in the kitchen after a bounce, you volley the next ball.

scene.alt: You stand inside the kitchen after hitting a bounced ball, and the next ball is coming in the air.

explanation.correct: Kitchen fault. You can enter the kitchen to hit a bounced ball, but you must exit before volleying again.
explanation.incorrect: The rule is clear: if you are in the kitchen, no volleys. You have to leave the zone before you can volley the next shot.
explanation.sayThisLine: In the kitchen? Hit groundstrokes only. Leave before volleying.

payload.prompt: You are in the kitchen after a bounce. What can you do?

options.text: Volley the next ball, since you are already in
Hit balls that have bounced, and step fully out before you volley
Leave the kitchen immediately or lose the point
Hit any shot, as long as you move back afterwards

explanation.correct: You can stay in the kitchen and keep hitting balls that have bounced. To volley, you have to get both feet out of the zone first.
explanation.incorrect: You are allowed to be in the kitchen, so there is no rush to leave. But volleying from inside is a fault, and moving back afterwards does not undo it.
explanation.sayThisLine: I can hit bounced balls from the kitchen, but I must step out to volley.

payload.prompt: Complete the kitchen entry rule.
payload.template: You may enter the kitchen to hit a {{ball-type}} ball, but you must {{action}} before volleying.

explanation.correct: You can enter the kitchen for a bounced ball, but you must leave the zone before you can volley again.
explanation.incorrect: The kitchen rule allows groundstrokes inside but forbids volleys. Exit, then volley.
explanation.sayThisLine: Bounce in kitchen? Go in. But exit before volleying again.

lessons.title: Reaching over
lessons.objective: Know paddle over the zone is fine if feet are outside.

payload.prompt: You stand outside the kitchen with both feet clear. Your paddle reaches over the kitchen line to volley.

scene.alt: You stand just behind the kitchen line while your paddle reaches out over the kitchen, in the air, to hit the ball.

explanation.correct: Legal. Your paddle can reach over the kitchen in the air as long as you are not touching the zone or its line when you hit.
explanation.incorrect: The fault is about touching the kitchen, not reaching over it. Your feet are clear, so a paddle in the air above the zone is fine.
explanation.sayThisLine: Reaching over the kitchen is fine if I am not touching it.

payload.ruleTag: Paddle reaching over kitchen is legal

payload.prompt: What decides whether a volley is a kitchen fault?

options.text: Whether your paddle reaches over the kitchen
Whether your arm crosses the kitchen line in the air
Whether you are touching the kitchen or its line
How hard you hit the ball

explanation.correct: It comes down to touching. Usually that is your feet, but it also counts if anything you wear or carry, like your paddle, touches the kitchen or its line while you volley.
explanation.incorrect: Reaching over the kitchen in the air is fine. The fault is about touching the zone or its line, and how hard you hit does not matter.
explanation.sayThisLine: Reaching over is fine. Touching the kitchen is the fault.

payload.prompt: Match each one to the kitchen volley rule.

pairs.definition: Cannot touch the kitchen or its line when you volley
Can reach over the kitchen, as long as it does not touch the zone
Cannot carry you into the kitchen after the volley

distractorDefinitions: Can only reach over the kitchen once per rally
Must stay behind the baseline at all times

explanation.summary: Reaching over the kitchen in the air is fine. What gets you in trouble is touching the zone or its line, and that includes being carried in by momentum after a volley.
explanation.sayThisLine: Reaching over is fine. Touching or drifting in is the fault.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I had to reach my paddle over the kitchen to volley. Was that a fault?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Not if your feet stayed out. Reaching over is fine; touching is the fault.
Yeah, you can't reach over the kitchen.
Yes, but only on a hard shot.
It depends on the angle of your paddle.

payload.translation: Sam reached a paddle over the kitchen without stepping in. That is legal: the fault is about touching the kitchen or its line, not about reaching over the air above it.

followUps.line: I think that's fine if your feet stayed out. Reaching over is okay, touching is the problem.
followUps.why: Clears up a common worry without sounding like an official.

followUps.line: Did you feel yourself drift in after? That would be the thing to watch for.
followUps.why: Shows you understand the momentum side as well.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Lots of new players think reaching over is a fault. Say it kindly: you are sharing a rule you just learned, not ruling on Sam's game.

lessons.title: Why the kitchen exists
lessons.objective: Explain the zone's purpose (no smashes at the net).

payload.prompt: Complete the reason for the kitchen.
payload.template: The kitchen stops players from {{action}} right at the net, which keeps rallies {{result}}.

explanation.correct: The kitchen stops players from standing at the net and smashing volleys. That keeps rallies longer and rewards patience and placement.
explanation.incorrect: Dinking and underhand serves are still allowed. What the kitchen removes is the power volley from right beside the net, and that is why rallies last.
explanation.sayThisLine: The kitchen stops net smashes, so rallies last longer.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Why can't I just rush the net and smash everything? I'm good at the net.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: That's what the kitchen is for: to keep net dominance from ending rallies.
You're not as good at the net as you think.
The kitchen rule is unfair to good volleyers.
Smashing is not allowed in pickleball.

payload.translation: Sam has just discovered the reason for the kitchen. It stops anyone from standing at the net and smashing, so patience and placement matter more than power.

followUps.line: Fair question! The kitchen is there so nobody can just camp at the net and smash.
followUps.why: Warm, and explains the reason without lecturing.

followUps.line: I think the kitchen makes it a game of patience and angles, not just who gets to the net first.
followUps.why: Offers your understanding as an opinion rather than a verdict.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You are explaining what you just learned, not teaching a class. A curious follow-up, like asking how Sam gets around a good net player, keeps it a conversation.

payload.prompt: What would happen to pickleball if there were no kitchen?

options.text: The game would be slower
Whoever reached the net first would smash and win
Soft shots would become more common
Serves would matter less

explanation.correct: Without the kitchen, the player who gets to the net first could volley hard at close range, which is very hard to defend. The game would become a race to the net.
explanation.incorrect: The kitchen exists to slow the net and encourage soft shots, so taking it away would do the opposite: more power, fewer long rallies.
explanation.sayThisLine: Without the kitchen it would be a race to the net, and smashes would win.

payload.prompt: You are at the net with a ball at your feet. Why should you dink instead of smashing?

situation.narrative: Your opponent sent a weak dink to the net. You are at the kitchen line and you could smash it.

facts.label: Your position
facts.value: At the net, in the kitchen

options.label: Smash it hard (if you could)
options.consequence: Smashing at the net would end every rally instantly. The game would reward net dominance alone, not strategy or skill.
considerations: Without the kitchen, power would rule
Soft play and angles would be pointless
Pickleball would become just about reaching the net

options.label: Dink soft (per the kitchen rule)
options.consequence: Dinking keeps the rally alive and forces your opponent to be patient. It's the heart of pickleball strategy and why the game is fun.
considerations: Dinking is the counter-strategy to the kitchen
It tests patience and angles, not just power
It's what separates pickleball from power sports

payload.expertNote: The kitchen makes dinking mandatory at the net. That's the whole point: soft play beats power in pickleball.
payload.sayThisLine: Kitchen forces soft play. That's what makes pickleball special.
